ai.definition: The Stellar Lifting Experiment is an experimental project aimed at developing technology capable of lifting matter from a star's surface, which can then be used in space propulsion systems.
ai.howItWorks: This experiment leverages quantum gravity principles and advanced materials to overcome the extreme gravitational forces on a star’s surface. The process involves creating localized regions where the effective gravitational force is reduced, allowing for the controlled lifting of small amounts of stellar material. This material can be used as fuel or reactants in space propulsion systems.
ai.problemSolved: The project addresses the challenge of developing sustainable and efficient space propulsion technologies that do not rely on traditional chemical fuels, which have limited energy density and are difficult to store and transport in space.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves creating specialized equipment capable of operating at stellar surface conditions. This includes advanced materials with high thermal stability and resistance to extreme radiation, as well as quantum gravity manipulation devices that can operate in vacuum environments.
ai.buildProcess: The build process starts with theoretical modeling and simulation to optimize the design for gravitational manipulation. Prototype testing is conducted under controlled laboratory conditions before moving on to full-scale experiments near stellar surfaces using robotic probes or satellites.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the development of advanced materials, high-energy quantum gravity manipulation devices, and the operational costs associated with sending equipment into space and maintaining it in harsh environments.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The project is currently in a very early stage, focusing on theoretical and experimental validation. There are no concrete plans for commercialization or widespread deployment at this time.
ai.regulation: Given the speculative nature of the technology, there are currently no specific regulations governing its development or use. However, any future implementation would likely require international agreements to manage potential space resource exploitation issues.
ai.risks: Technical risks include the unpredictability of quantum gravity effects and the extreme environmental conditions near stars. Safety risks involve the potential for catastrophic failure during experiments that could damage equipment or pose hazards to nearby spacecraft.
ai.profitability: At this stage, profitability is not a relevant metric as the technology has not yet reached a point where it can be commercialized. However, successful development could lead to significant long-term benefits in space exploration and propulsion technologies.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development may involve refining theoretical models, improving materials science, and conducting more extensive experimental testing near stellar surfaces. Collaboration with other space agencies or private companies might also accelerate progress.
ai.energyRequirements: Field units draw low hundreds of watts; fabrication is energy-intensive due to vacuum baking and material synthesis processes.

glossary.def: A hypothetical theory in physics that unifies quantum mechanics with general relativity, potentially allowing for the manipulation of gravitational forces at a microscopic scale.
The outermost layer of a star where most physical and chemical processes occur. The conditions are extremely harsh, with intense radiation and high temperatures.

subsystems.name: Flux-tube coupler
subsystems.role: anchors a magnetic loop into the star's own field so plasma can rise along field lines instead of fighting gravity unaided.

subsystems.name: Lift driver
subsystems.role: supplies the energy that pushes plasma up out of the star's gravity well.
parts: energy source (star's own radiation, beamed power, or onboard reactor)

subsystems.name: Transport channel
subsystems.role: carries plasma away from the star at hundreds of kilometres per second.

subsystems.name: Capture station
subsystems.role: intercepts the stream and turns it into storable material.

subsystems.name: Separation plant
subsystems.role: splits hydrogen, helium and heavier elements such as metals and rare isotopes.

subsystems.name: Propellant and power conversion
subsystems.role: feeds the harvested material to thrusters or reactors.

buildSteps.title: Characterise the star
buildSteps.detail: Remote missions and ground telescopes map the magnetic field, active regions and wind output over a full activity cycle to find where a flux tube could anchor.

buildSteps.title: Reproduce a flux tube in the lab
buildSteps.detail: Scale experiments on Earth recreate a magnetised plasma column and study how it can be driven and guided without instability.

buildSteps.title: Fly a close-in test probe
buildSteps.detail: An uncrewed craft survives for months in the inner corona, measuring heat flux, particle density and magnetic geometry at the intended anchor point.

buildSteps.title: Anchor the magnetic loop
buildSteps.detail: A coil array is positioned so its field connects with the star's field lines, forming a continuous channel from the surface layers to the collection point.

buildSteps.title: Drive the plasma up
buildSteps.detail: Energy is injected at the base of the channel, boosting plasma pressure so the star's gas flows outward along the flux tube instead of escaping as ordinary wind.

buildSteps.title: Guide and accelerate
buildSteps.detail: A magnetic nozzle and coil stages accelerate the stream outward while it expands and cools, keeping it off every solid surface.

buildSteps.title: Capture, separate and store
buildSteps.detail: The collection station brakes the stream magnetically, radiates away the leftover heat, separates elements and stores propellant.

buildSteps.title: Scale to an engineered wind
buildSteps.detail: Many loops operating together would let the extraction rate be dialled up or down — and would slowly change the star's own mass and lifetime.

prerequisites.why: the physics is observed in the Sun's corona and studied in lab plasmas, but nobody has steered a flux tube deliberately.
coils must stay superconducting within a few stellar radii, facing intense heat, particle flux and radiation.
spacecraft have flown close to the Sun, but none has operated for years at the flux levels a lifting station would see.
coil arrays and collection stations of this size must be built in orbit from many launches.

prerequisites.tech: Plasma cooling and cryogenic storage in space
prerequisites.why: storing hydrogen and helium as propellant requires radiators and insulation that have never been built at this scale.

pathway.milestone: solar physics missions mapping the magnetic field, wind and coronal heating
pathway.unlocks: the basic data any lifting design depends on.

pathway.milestone: magnetic-scoop concepts that harvest the natural stellar wind rather than lifting from the surface
pathway.unlocks: tests of capture, cooling and storage without needing to force plasma off the star.

pathway.milestone: a probe anchored inside the corona for years
pathway.unlocks: proof that magnets, materials and power systems can survive there.

pathway.milestone: a first working flux tube lifting small amounts of stellar material to a depot
pathway.unlocks: propellant and reaction mass sourced from the star itself, with no mining or launch from a planet.

pathway.milestone: industrial-scale lifting multiple loops, deliberately altering the star's outflow
pathway.unlocks: star-scale resource use — and a hard choice, since removing mass changes the star's brightness and lifespan.
